messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan was thirty-two, a park ranger in the Pacific Northwest, when he was abducted during a routine patrol on a remote trail. For three days his captors held him in an abandoned hunting cabin, beating him, threatening him with a knife, and leaving him bound in darkness for hours before he finally escaped when a hiker stumbled onto the cabin. In the hospital he could not put the ordeal into words—the police asked what happened and he lost the thread, certain moments blindingly clear while whole stretches remained blank, and that inability to explain only deepened his conviction that his body had been permanently damaged, that something inside him had been broken forever. He found that the very belief that he was broken seemed to keep him anchored to the sharpest images—the knife, the darkness—as if his mind was determined to show him exactly where the damage had begun, making those moments loom so large that the rest of the event felt unreal. He began to rehearse every conversation before it happened, hoping to sound normal and hide the cracks; the more he rehearsed, the more the actual memory felt like a story he was telling about someone else, the clear images slipping further away, the blanks filling with what he had practiced instead of what had really occurred.

His sense of physical vulnerability also infected how he experienced the world. He came to believe he could not rely on other people—after all, no one had come for him—and so any small delay in his daily routine felt catastrophic. If a hiker was late returning from a trailhead, his body would react before his thoughts could catch up: his chest would tighten, his hands would shake, and he would be certain something terrible had happened. He found himself checking and rechecking the locks on the visitor-center doors every night, sometimes three or four times, because the feeling of danger never quite left him. The constant threat monitoring made his memory even more fragmented—when he tried to recall the cabin, the blank spots seemed to grow, and the clear moments like the knife blade loomed so large that the rest no longer seemed real.

To manage this unrelenting pressure, Ethan began to numb his feelings. He stopped feeling the sharp edges of fear, but also joy and connection; he became emotionally flat, which he told himself was easier. He avoided driving whenever possible—being a passenger was even worse, because being trapped in a moving vehicle felt like a reenactment of captivity—and he started asking coworkers to cover the distant trailheads by truck. The avoidance made his world smaller, and the more he avoided, the more threatening any unavoidable driving became; his body would start to react before he even turned the key, reinforcing his belief that he could not trust himself. He rehearsed conversations with his supervisor to explain why he could no longer patrol certain areas, and the rehearsing itself made him feel as though he was losing his hold on reality—another symptom that he might be going crazy. Each compulsive check of a door lock confirmed that he was unsafe, each numb hour proved that he was damaged, and each failed attempt to describe what happened convinced him that his mind was permanently scarred.

By the time he sought help at a veterans’ clinic—he was not a veteran, but the local therapist had experience with trauma—Ethan had stopped hiking entirely on his days off, stopped seeing the few friends he had, and was barely functioning at work. He came because he had been caught rehearsing the same apology to a visitor three times in a row, and the visitor had stared at him with concern. What frightened him most was the thought that if anyone truly saw what was inside his head, they would confirm what he already suspected: that he was broken beyond repair. He hoped, quietly, that someone might prove him wrong.
